utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I greet the parties and the accused and the interpreters. We are now going to resume with our work with Witness LL who can now also be brought in. Would the usher please have the witness brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. If I could introduce Ms. Alinde Verhaag she is temporarily replacing Emile Van der Does, our case manager, who is absent today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, then we agree this new replacement. (Witness LL entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness LL, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Are you all rested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, then let us continue then. Witness LL (continued) Examined by MR. CAYLEY (continued):

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Witness LL. If you could continue the account of events that you were giving yesterday from the end of May 1993, when I believe HVO soldiers came to your house in Gromiljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday I stopped with the incident when an HVO soldier beat me up because of my son's car, when I went to UNPROFOR to make a complaint and when a Canadian officer came there and when we -- several of us, when we lodged a complaint. Since the HVO soldiers had already broken into my house on one occasion, I was frightened, I was too scared to sleep alone in the house and, therefore, before the curfew on the 31st May 1993, I went to sleep at my neighbour's house. On the next morning, that is on 1st June, when I came back home, I saw that the doors were broken and that the house had been robbed and that most of my belongings had been taken away. I managed to learn from my neighbours, who were there in the immediate vicinity and who were watching from their window, that everything had been taken away by my neighbours. So I went to work and after I finished working, I went to the police station in Kiseljak to see the Chief of Police. I told him what had happened and he said that one of their inspectors, an HVO crime inspector, should go over to my house and inspect the scene. So, we took his car and we went back to my house. He inspected everything and made a report. He advised me to repair the locks, which I did the following day. I think that the locks were repaired during the afternoon hours, before the evening, and sometime around the curfew -- or rather after the curfew, a vehicle with HVO plates on it arrived and four HVO soldiers got off the car and they went upstairs. I remained on the ground floor, and since it was forbidden for us Muslims to switch on the lights, I remained behind the curtain and I managed, somehow, in spite of that, to recognise some of them. They started breaking the door and as they were doing that upstairs, around the rooms, I managed to jump out of the window on the back side of the house and I hid in the garden. After that, they went downstairs. They broke down the remaining doors and they started taking our things -- taking furniture out. I remained hidden in the grass and I observed all that, and when I was sure that they had left, I went to my neighbour's house to spend the night there. I went back home on the next morning and I realised that my house had been vandalised and demolished; that eight doors were completely out of their frames and I saw that the tiles in the bathroom were all smashed. During the first robbery they took all my food, so I did not have any food at home. For several days I remained without food, so people from the village brought me some food. After the second robbery, I went to the police station in Kiseljak again and I told the Chief of Police what had happened. However, he did not say anything to that. From there, I went to the HVO barracks. I wanted to find Mr. Ivica Rajic, commander of the HVO, because I wanted to tell him what was happening, but he refused to see me. After that, from the barracks, I went to the Town Hall to see Mr. Jozo Boro, who was the president of the municipality and president of the HVO at the time, so I told him what was happening to me and to other Muslims, but he remained silent. He did make a few notes in his notebook, but he made no comment whatsoever. This is where I saw Vinko Antunovic. He held a very high position within the HVO, so I complained to him as well. However, he left me in the middle of a sentence. So, I returned home and until 5th October, I did not spend a single night in my house. During the day I would spend some time in the house and around the house, after I would come back from work. Every day the local commander would come by, the local commander of the HVO police, Josip Maric. He mistreated us -- he harassed us rather, by ordering his subordinates to fire around our houses during the night, or by simply threatening us, interrogating us as to the whereabouts of our family members. He abused us verbally and this went on every day. He even took part in the looting of some houses. On 21st June, when I came to work, a colleague of mine arrived and she told me that the manager of the institution, of the company, had sent a message to me and a few other Muslims who were still working there, and the message was that we should no longer come to work -- that we no longer needed to come to work because he had received an order from the HVO to expel us. They did not give us any documents about that; they did not give us -- they did not return to us any documentation that we had. So, from 2nd June until 17th July, when I was expelled from my house, HVO soldiers came to my house on 13 occasions. They would bring some Croats with them because they wanted to move them into my house and to expel me. Since the HVO authorities of the municipality of Kiseljak had appointed an official commission which, together with the military police, evicted Muslims from their houses, they told me -- they told us that we should not leave our houses in their absence, that we should wait for them. So, every time they would come to my house to evict me from my house, I always requested that it be an official eviction. On 17th July 1993, in the morning, at about 6.30, three HVO soldiers came to my house. They were all armed and were accompanied by three HVO policemen who were also armed. So, they stood in front of my house and the local commander, the person I have already mentioned, Josip Maric, entered my house, and he told me to leave the house because some Croats were supposed to move in. Since I knew him, I kindly asked him not to do that, but he simply started beating me, over my face with his fist and he twisted my arm around my back -- behind my back and he thus evicted me from my house. He cursed me, he cursed my Turkish mother and he kept saying to these other HVO soldiers: "Kill her. Throw her into the river, into the creek." After that he left, and when I asked those who remained -- who had remained -- when I asked them where I was supposed to go now, one of them, an HVO soldier came closer and he, too, started hitting me on the head and then he pushed me down and I fell and he started kicking me all over my body, and the others just remained standing. They kept abusing me verbally, swearing and cursing, and after he had finished beating me, he said: "Do not dare come close to your house because there is a huge knife waiting for you there". I had no shoes on, just my stockings and I had very little clothes on, and since I did not know where to go, I went to the UNPROFOR base. This UNPROFOR base had recently been established in Gromiljak and this is where I reported my case, and I wanted to know where I could go. Then an UN official contacted the Kiseljak command, the headquarters in Kiseljak, and they told him that I should remain with the UNPROFOR in the vicinity of the base and that they would come as soon as possible and take care of me and try to resolve my situation. After a few hours, Captain Craig Carrington arrived together with the chief of the HVO police. So we started talking. Since the Chief of Police used to live in Gromiljak, we knew each other and I asked him if they had any further plans with me. So, he offered me his house. At that time, his house was empty because his family was in Split, but I did not accept it and I wanted him to get me back to my house. But he said it was impossible, because some Croats were supposed to live in my house. Then he offered me to Muslim houses and these houses were earmarked as some kind of collective accommodation for the displaced Muslims and I agreed to go to one of them, provided that they send me a certificate -- that they actually sent a certificate to the owner of the house and to the commander of the HVO, Maric, whereby they would ensure that we would not be harassed or evicted from that house. He promised to do that and, on the next day, he did, indeed, send such a certificate. Mr. Craig Carrington gave me his card -- I have it here -- and he told me that, should I have any problems that I can always look for him -- look him up. So I moved to that house and I spent there two and-a-half months. That house was in the immediate vicinity of my house, so I could watch those Croats who were unknown to me every day. I could watch them living in my house, enjoying my house, which was, of course, very difficult for me. Mr. Maric kept coming on a daily basis and he ordered us that we do not go into the backyard, that we were under house arrest and that we were going to be sent to a camp. On four or five occasions, the HVO soldiers came in a van and told to everybody in the house to get ready within five minutes, that they would take us to the Rotilj camp. And then, a few minutes later, somebody else would show up and they would say: "Go back into the house, you are not going to go to the camp today". This went on until 5th October 1993, when I was exchanged and transferred to the free territory. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness LL. I think that the Prosecutor has a few clarifications or a few questions he would like to put to you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please, Mr. President. Witness LL, was there a mosque in the village of Gromiljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of what happened to that mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After a while, after the HVO attack, after the mosque had been looted, it was set on fire, but since there was a Croat house nearby, the Croats put out the fire and then, in February of 1994, after the Washington Agreement was signed, the mosque was completely blown up and the other mosques in other surrounding villages were all destroyed after the Washington Agreement. Some had been destroyed before, but after the Washington Agreement they were blown up and not a single one remained. And people would find copies of Koran and other religious objects from these mosques strewn around, sometimes thrown into the creek, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness LL, am I right in saying that the HVO set the mosque on fire after the attack in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in your testimony the fate of an elderly couple who lived in the village, an 80 year old couple. Can you explain to the court what happened to their house and what the HVO did to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 18th April 1993, after those explosions were heard first, the houses in Visnjica were set on fire and then later on there was this elderly couple, Imamovic. They were retirees, they had no sons, they had no males in the house and they lived alone, so they set their house on fire first and we saw the flames coming up and across from their house. The HVO soldiers knocked on Halid Begovic's house, his son opened up, he asked what they wanted, they shot at him. His father stepped out to protect him. He was hit in the back and then the HVO soldiers left and the two of them managed somehow to go into the basement. They had a store down there and they managed to hide behind some goods there. And then they -- the HVO set their house on fire later on, but they managed to crawl out and save themselves. Below there, there was another house which was also set on fire twice and it finally burned down, and during the time when these houses in Gomjanica were being set on fire, we would count them, and every night we would count 10 to 12 houses on fire. First, they would loot them. We saw the HVO soldiers driving away goods on trucks, so they first looted them, then they set them on fire. The population managed to flee to the hills and then, across the hills, they managed to escape to Visoko. Some of the people were killed there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness LL, you said that on 31st May of 1993 your house was looted by your neighbours. Were you referring to your neighbours who were in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were all wearing uniforms and they all carried weapons. And whatever was done was done by the neighbours, not by unknown persons, I know all these peoples' first and last names and, if needed, I can name them all. I asked one of them: "How long is this going to go on?", and he said: "Until we have killed all the Muslims in Kiseljak." They said they were given a free reign to do whatever they wanted to us without answering for that to anyone. These were their words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You recall earlier I showed you a video clip in which you identified a man who beat you at your house before you were evicted; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that clip could be shown now, please? It is part of Exhibit 260. If, Witness LL, you could identify to the court the man who beat you? We will play it a number of times, if necessary. If that clip could be played, please? (Video clip played).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you see it on the TV screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is the man that beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is the covered -- this man. (Indicating). Josip Maric. This one here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we play it again, please? Could you describe the position of this man, because the judges cannot see what you are pointing at? Is it the man with the silver hair on the far right-hand corner of the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next to the flagpole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is his name again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Josip Maric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the man who beat you at your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: On the left, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can play it again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I want to be clear who it is who you are talking about. You talked about a silver haired person, both of them are wearing hats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is the man in the distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will indicate to you, Mr. President. You see the gentleman with the white hair to the right of the flagpole?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: To the very right, yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that correct, Witness LL?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And he did not beat only me, he beat some other women as well. (Video clip continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is fine, thank you. Finally, if the witness could be shown Exhibit 313. (Handed). I will wait for you to get your spectacles out. Witness LL, just to give the judges a geographical reference, is that the location of your village which is ringed in a black circle on this map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions of the witness, Mr. President. If the two exhibits could be admitted into evidence, Exhibit 313, which is the map, and Exhibit 314, which is the clip from Exhibit 260.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So 260 is already admitted, although it was admitted with some objections, so now this is only an excerpt, I do not think we need to give it any number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My colleague has just suggested, Mr. President, that we label it Exhibit 260A -- 260B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I share the opinion of the Office of the Prosecutor because, Mr. Registrar, we need to be able to refer to this particular exhibit, otherwise we will have to go back to the transcript to find out whether or not this was targeted as an actual exhibit. So let us, then, go not back to the previous number, but this number as it corresponds to the clip shown to this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Very yes, very well. In this case, let us give it the letter "B", because a document has already been presented before another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I do not know, do what is necessary. The problem is that we must have a clear reference and that this be annexed to the testimony given by Witness LL. Without further delay, excuse it, Witness LL, there are no other observations, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no other observations, Mr. President, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You should understand that now we are going to give the floor to the Defence for General Blaskic and it is now the Defence counsel that is going to now put to you a number of questions, Mr. Nobilo, perhaps. Cross-examined by MR. NOBILO:

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon Witness LL.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you heard, I would like to ask you a few questions. In the beginning of your testimony, you spoke about some kind of growing distance or start of maybe hatred between the Croats and Muslims, and you mentioned that there were some educated people who were spreading these feelings. Can you tell us; when did this start? When did this process of separation between the Croats and the Muslims start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right after the elections of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the time went on, were these just exceptions, as you pointed out, just the more educated people engaged in this, or did it spread towards the general population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say that a larger number of Croats, or most of the Croats, expressed these views against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean? A largest number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, even children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there those who tried to keep the old kind of relationships?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who tried to keep the old type of relationships complained to us that they were under pressure from the HVO to not communicate with us. So they apologised to us, those with whom we socialised more. They just said that they did not dare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to you, these were in the minority, such people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard from a lot of people that this was a general attitude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this: did this attitude then produce a certain reaction, apart of the Muslims that were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we wanted to keep the old relationships because, traditionally, we had very good relations between Croats and Muslims and you know that there was even a coalition, the flags of the HVO and the SDA were sort of joined, so nobody really expected this to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that business premises were destroyed. Can you place it in time? What time was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in 1992, in the beginning, in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the first half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes and it escalated when the Serbs attacked, when the war in Bosnia broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see an act of destruction of any of these business premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not an eye-witness to any of those, but I saw the result of it shortly thereafter, and everyone talked about it. As I mentioned yesterday, I saw a shoe shop owned by a man, and it was a very nice shop with very expensive Italian shoes. It had metal bars in the window and the HVO soldiers brought a tractor; they fixed a chain to it, they pulled it out, they broke the window and the Croatian population stormed the shoe shop and took away all the shoes. I arrived shortly thereafter and I saw the whole place ransacked and all the -- all glass was smashed, et cetera. There were even jokes being made how certain women changed the shoe size because the original ones did not fit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About the HVO soldiers pulling out the bars, did you see that or did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I only heard about it from others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you are speaking quite quickly, please think about the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Apart from this case, in other cases, those who told you about what happened, were those people eye-witnesses to, let us say, break-ins, or they too heard it from someone else yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody talked about it, it was biggest topic of the day. It was not just the shoe shop, it was also the butcher's shop, there was also a cafe owned by a Muslim and another store. They looted the merchandise there and people saw that and this was what was discussed among the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, can you tell me: did you personally hear this from an eye-witness or from someone who had already heard about it from someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure about that any more because this was a long time ago, but the fact is that this took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about Merhamet? It was a warehouse, right of the relief organisation, it was set on fire, you told us and you heard this was done by the HVO soldiers. That is what you said. I have a similar question for you: did you hear that from a person who was an eye-witness to it or from someone who also heard it from someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I was at work and I was in the backyard of the company where I was working, or the institution where I was working, and then there was some fire there, some people had been injured and they were brought in the vicinity of where I could see them. Then they were that the building organisation where Merhamet was, they said it was destroyed but there were also problems with Merhamet. There were often times when these merchandise was coming in. It was often looted and we got very few things while the Croats were getting many more things, that we only got very basic things, barely enough to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, these injured persons who told you about this, did they tell you that they knew who set these explosives there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said that this was the HVO soldiers who set the explosives there. Because the Muslims already had restricted movements. The Muslim men were mostly in the barracks, they were sent to dig trenches, they could not move around town freely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this explosion was before 18th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move to 18th April 1993. You said that the commander of the village, Velimir Milicevic, requested that all Muslims should gather at eight o'clock in one of their neighbour's houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the basement, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in the basement. Was that in order for them to be protected from the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because the men who came to inform us about that, he said that if you do not show up, you will all be arrested. If you intend to protect someone, you do not threaten him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Madam, you gave a statement previously to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal. On page 2 of the statement, the beginning of paragraph 2, you stated the following: "In the afternoon of 18th April 1993, a Croat came to my house and informed me that his commander, Velimir Milicevic, wanted all the Muslims to come to the house of a Croat neighbour named Jozo Biletic at 6.00 pm, so that we would be protected from the shelling." Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. A woman who was present there at the house, he asked why we had to go to the basement and this is what he said. However, later on he said that if we failed to appear on our own will that they would come to arrest us. Then it was perfectly clear for me what he really meant. If you want to protect someone, you are not going to arrest him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any shelling at that time of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The incident you told us about when your dog was killed and when they planned to steal your son's car, were these people your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any quarrels with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were guards in your village during the night, HVO guards, there was also curfew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this all in order to protect you from the incursions of criminals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did they have guards, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To prevent us from fleeing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have any guards during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you move around freely during the day, could you go to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could. Only 15 days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time while you were prevented from moving around freely, were there any military operations going on at that time, during the first week following 18th April 1993? Was there any fighting going on in the surrounding villages? Could you hear the shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we could hear the shooting but there were no -- there was no fighting going on, because in order to fight you need to have two parties. It was not an ordinary war. The BiH Army was not there. They had no-one to fight. They knew very well that they -- that Muslims had no weapons and that is why they attacked the village. They knew very well at the time where the BiH soldiers were deployed. At that time, the BiH soldiers were in the area of Koscan and Kralupi, they were holding lines against Serbs and they knew perfectly well that we had no-one to protect us. Because, on 17th April, on the eve of the attack against Muslims, Kiseljak Radio informed their population, their residents, they told them that they should stay calm if they heard some shooting on the next day because UNPROFOR was supposed to have some kind of exercise. So they carried out an attack and the attack was followed by ethnic cleansing and evictions. After that, it was forbidden for all of us to move around freely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear this personally, did you hear what was announced over the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not hear that personally. Some other people did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But even if you have shooting coming from only one side, how long did it last, for how many days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, it lasted for a couple of days, but since nobody returned fire, since there was no-one there, no-one to counterattack, they set about burning houses. So lots of houses were on fire at that time. We could count them every evening. There were about 10 or 12 houses on fire and then, on the first -- when the HVO forces were perfectly sure that there would be no reaction or response, they attacked the village. They tried to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present there when it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went home from work and I was stopped at the barricade and around 2.00 pm, the shelling of the village started and lots of people were killed. And from that day on, HVO soldiers had the village of Gomionica under their control and they hoisted a huge flag on the hill above the village. You could see this Croatian flag from distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then sum-up: for how many days could you hear the shooting after 18th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did not count the days, but it was -- it lasted for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw that man in your son's car, was that a neighbour of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he did not live in the immediate vicinity of my house, but he comes from the same area and I used to know him. He was an HVO soldier, I knew him by name and maybe two or three days before that I even spoke to him in one of my neighbour's houses, so when I told Commander Maric that that man had taken my son's car, Maric told me that it was he, himself, who gave him permission to do that and he said that not a single Muslim could have -- could own a car any more, so everything was taken away from us. Nobody had anything, not a single vehicle, car or tractor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this man from the same village as you are, this man who took your son's car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he is not from the same village, he is from a neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that after the 18th April 1993, that Muslim men had to report twice a day in the morning and in the evening at the Gromiljak police station so that they would not escape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know that for sure because my family members also had to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are two men -- two males -- in your family? I am not going to mention their names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they flee to the territory under the BiH control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the attack of the 18th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to see the Chief of Police, when you first reported what had happened in your house, did you sign any report or a statement? Did you sign anything that was in written form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Detective Vukoja, who carried out an on-site investigation of the break-in of my house, he made the report of that and he told me that I should come to the police station to sign it. However, when I came to the police station, one policeman would not let me in, this policeman's name was Rade Rebuz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that four HVO soldiers, on the night when you hid in the garden, that four HVO soldiers came to your house and demolished the interior of your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know them personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you on good terms with them or did you have any problems with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have any problems with anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, I am sorry. Would you please turn towards the judges when you respond to the questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can turn to listen to the question, turn your head towards the Defence, of course that is required. When you answer, please turn towards the judges, thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When the manager of your company told you that you should leave your work, you said that he had received an order from the HVO. Did he give you any names; the names of persons in authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not mention any names. He did not tell us that himself, he simply sent a colleague of ours who then told us that the manager had received an order from HVO authorities, that we should no longer come to work because they no longer needed us. So, my group was among the last ones that left the company. It happened on 21st June and they no longer called us, they did not give us any release documents or anything. But this is what was told, that we should leave work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, when he said HVO authorities, how did you understand that? Was that the local government of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the local government of Kiseljak and the President of the HVO was Jozo Boro, he was the first man, the most important person as far as civilian authorities are concerned, as far as I know it was Mr. Rajic who was the military leader in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there was a commission for evictions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the exact title of that commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for me its title was "the Commission for Evictions". It had several members. There was one person who used to work in the Forestry, one other person who used to work in the Land Survey Department and a third person who was the owner of a shop. So they used to go round in a police vehicle; they had some forms with them, so whenever they would evict us Muslims, they would give us some kind of written decisions, some kind of paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they call themselves, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know. However, this commission was under the authority of the municipality. There was no private initiative in that regard. I know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me who it was that moved into your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. People from the municipality of Fojnica, then Majic and Bosniak families. Two families moved into my house, one family used to live downstairs and the other one upstairs. I do not know whether I should say this, but these people very primitive. I could see that from the way they treated me, the way they abused me verbally and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not have to give us their names for your own protection, but could you tell us how come that they had come from Fojnica to live in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that they were evacuated from their village because apparently they were scared, they were being threatened by some Mujehadeens, so they took advantage of that. These young people did not want to go to war and apparently that is why they fled. That is what they told us, these people from Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people from Fojnica, were they Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of the Chief of Police, it was a public office, it is not going to reveal your identity. Could you then tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a person by the name Velimir Milicevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly did he tell you, why was he not able to return you to your house, because he obviously liked you, he wanted to do something for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think you are right. His house was just across the headquarters and Josip Maric was there, the person who beat me, so I was a perfect target for them, and he said that I could go to his house because he was embarrassed because of the presence of Mr. Craig Carrington, who heard it all. I first talked to Velimir Milicevic in our language and when the interpreter tried to interpret, I interfered and I managed with my English to tell Mr. Carrington what had happened and Mr. Velimir Milicevic was shocked because he did not expect me to be able to communicate in English. So that is why he offered me his house, but I refused it because I would have been a perfect target for his policemen. Then I did not want to go to his house because I had a house of my own, but then he said I could not go back to my house because how some Croats were supposed to live there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he specific? Did he say which Croats from which town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the mosque had been set on fire. Did you know who had set it on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, but I can claim -- I am sure that it was not Muslims, because there were no Muslims there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that in a number of villages in the municipality of Kiseljak, mosques were being demolished and destroyed after the Washington Agreement by Croats. Could you state the names of such villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hercezi, for example, Visnjica, all the neighbouring villages, the surrounding villages of Gromiljak. I cannot remember any other villages but I know I heard that maybe four or five mosques had been destroyed in addition to the mosque in Gromiljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we are talking about six or seven mosques that were demolished after the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew your Croat neighbours very well. Am I right in thinking that almost every adult Croat, every male, had a weapon and a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You lived, for a very long time, together with your Croat neighbours, you also used to work with them. Am I right in thinking that almost every adult Croat, male Croat at that time had a weapon and a uniform --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am objecting at this point. This is completely outside the scope of the examination-in-chief. This matter was never addressed by me in my examination and would I ask that counsel move on to his next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness, on several occasions, spoke about her neighbours wearing uniforms. These were Croats who were members of the HVO and allegedly they did this or that and my question to her was: were these uniformed males majority or minority in that area?, so I do not understand why this would be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I think you stated a question, that was stated differently from what you put it the first time. That was the one objected to. If you want to put that question again, go ahead in the way you just did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. It is the same point: adult Croat males who were your neighbours, did they all, or most of them, have uniforms and weapons, the ones that you knew in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, even women. Even women. I know that the women who worked, who were from Kiseljak, were taken to certain locations to train in firing from automatic weapons, so that they would shoot balijas, which was a bad word for Muslims. They were also seen wearing uniforms and coming back home at night after shooting practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us try to synthesise, if I could ask you for an opinion. However, there is an additional question my colleague just passed to me. Was your exchange a private one, or was it done through official channels of both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a private exchange, it went through the Office for Exchange and with the assistance of the European Monitors, and I also have certificate that I was exchanged and who I was exchanged through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was exchanged for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a small group, it was six Muslims for six Croats, and there were Croats who did not want to be exchanged, who wanted to stay behind in their houses, so there were six women there and we were also six women; that is, two girls and four women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who asked for this exchange, you or someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the very beginning when I started being persecuted, I asked to be exchanged, to go to the free territory, even if they took my house, so that I could be reunited with my family. However, I failed to mention one thing: the HVO started expelling Muslims from downtown Kiseljak first, they would just catch people in the streets, they would take them to the barricade, then they would expel them, even people who were handicapped, they carried them in blankets and they would bring them to the road and would force them to go. Then they were taking money and gold in order to get people across the lines and across the barricades onto the free territory because there were times when the army was not manning the -- later on, this was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please do not review information of a personal nature, Mr. Nobilo. All right, Mr. Registrar, I think we should strike those particular elements from the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Maybe it is enough that we say that she lives in a Croat house, and that Croats are living in her house in Kiseljak. Maybe we can just redact the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we have taken protective measures, so when any identifying information is not revealed, what do you think of this, Mr. Cayley? Perhaps you did not follow what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I did. I understood that, essentially, the witness identified the village where she was living. Both parties have to attempt not to ask questions. I cannot keep hitting the button every time Mr. Nobilo gives identifying features about the witness. I agree that that part of the evidence has to be stricken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am not asking you to jump up each time a question comes to that area. I am the one that raised this particular issue. The question I am asking you now is: I felt that we should take out this particular element on this point. I am asking your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Hayman also seems to agree. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I did not understand, is only the name of the village going to be redacted, or the entire answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The point that will be stricken is the point concerning her current residence. Indeed, statements about not only the village but the house in which she lives. I prefer that this information not be revealed since it is of a personal nature. This was something we had already decided and agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Then I would just like to rephrase the question so that we avoid any identification of any sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness LL, I am going to ask you to look at this and to know that this has been stricken from the record. You should know that there are not many people here in the room -- rather in the gallery, but these people, of course, are people who are subjected to professional secrets and to keeping these secrets, so please go on with cross-examination, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. I am almost done. Can we just say that you now live in a Croat house and Croats are now living in a Muslim house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, very well. In closing, can you just synthesise as your opinion -- I do not know if this is outside of the scope -- but you live there for a long time, you are an educated person. Tell me: could Croats and Muslims live there together now? Have they overcome this hatred, or is the hatred still there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may be biased of me to say that the Croats -- that the Muslims are more tolerant that others, with other religions, but I believe that the Croats in Kiseljak do not want us to come back. I think that even today they work on us not returning there. I can mention that the programme of the return of refugees has started and Muslims are starting to clear the rubble of their destroyed homes so that the donors could come and see this and offer assistance. However, a most extreme person in Kiseljak is showing around. He is showing up with revolver and he is threatening people, so I am not sure that this hatred is going to disappear that easily. I can say that I do not harbour any hatred. I pity people who have declared themselves in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well, thank you, Witness LL. Mr. President, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, do you have any questions? Re-examined by MR. CAYLEY:

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, just one point, Mr. President. Witness LL, it is concerning the mosque in Gromiljak, was the mosque in Gromiljak initially set fire to by the HVO in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are now going to receive questions from the judges, Witness LL. I will begin first with the judge to my right, Judge Riad. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Witness LL. I would like to ask you a few questions to make things a little bit clear in my mind. You mentioned that on 31st May 1993, can you remember after the curfew, four HVO soldiers came to your house, went upstairs and you watched them. You recognised some of them while hiding in the grass, they vandalised the house and they even demolished and smashed the tiles and the story goes on. Was there any reason, in your opinion, why you were specially selected for this, what you call "vandalism and destruction", and before your son's car was stolen? I do not want you to be specific, just a general answer. Was it because you were a resistant or was it because of your status in society or was it a systematic way against anybody? Were you anybody or were you somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that I enjoyed a certain amount of reputation in this area and there was no reason for anyone to exact any revenge against me. I was nice to people and they were nice to me. I think that the main reason for it all was looting because this area -- especially the Gomionica and Gromiljak, the Muslim population was very industrious and they had a lot of property and belonging, we had good furniture, good cars and so now that was targeted. I think that there was no special reason, maybe somebody had something against my going to report this. I could see that as the only reason, but I believe that otherwise my ethnic background may have been the main reason for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was that done to other people in the same way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe that among women I was the one who was the most targeted, in this village that is, and Mr. Josip Maric, the local police chief, also beat other women and taking their property, expelling them from the house and abused them otherwise, so I am not the only one. So, I was not the exclusive target. Others suffered too, but I may have been targeted also because I showed more courage maybe and they did not like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did this Mr. Maric have anything against you in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. Before the attack he was quite nice to me. In fact, we would sit down and have coffee together and when we would meet each other he would smile broadly. He was really very polite. I think it was some kind of a mask. I only realised who this person was when I heard in 1992 that he beat prisoners in the Kaonik prison in 1992. He used to be a policeman beforehand, so he retired as a policeman, he took an early retirement, then he went back into an active duty when the hostilities broke out, so he went to this camp and he beat prisoners there, so I tried to keep distance from this man after I heard that. Later, when he came to threaten us that we were not allowed to go out of the house and after all the beatings and after all the abuse that he exposed me to, he was still saying "good day" to me and being nice, so that is hypocrisy. To me, that is real hypocrisy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you saw that people who came to your house, you recognised some of them. They were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then you said that other houses were looted and things were stolen and taken away on trucks. Was this military trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not military trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Taken away by HVO --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, right. Those who were taking things and driving them away were wearing the HVO uniforms and they had the insignia on their sleeves. I can name them, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So, you went and complained to the Chief of Police. Was the Chief of Police the superior of this Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Who was the superior of Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Velimir Milicevic. That was the person to whom I went to complain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What was his title or role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Velimir Milicevic was the Chief of the HVO police. He was the superior officer there. And Mr. Josip Maric was a local police commander or chief in the village of Gromiljak and Mr. Milicevic was the overall head of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you think of complaining to the headquarters of the HVO, to go to Vitez and complain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How far were you from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure, but maybe about 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that there was an old couple, 80 years old, whose house was set on fire and they died, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted), whereas the old couple they both died as refugees some time later, but their house is no longer around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it the HVO who did all that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that finally you asked somebody: "Where are we supposed to go?", and they told you: "We want to kill all Muslims", then they mentioned that they were given -- I think this is the English translation -- free reign to do whatever they wanted with Muslims with impunity, they can do anything with the Muslims. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told this by Bonifacije Milicevic called Bono he was also a member of the HVO organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it his own version or do you think that he spoke in the name of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he spoke in the name, or on behalf of, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said that the hostility started after the elections of 1991, and you mentioned even that you had to go to work on foot, no bus would take you, and so on. How did you see this hostility growing? What moved it? Was there a kind of propaganda, brainwash? What changed the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that it was exactly that, propaganda, because through my job I was known to most people in the municipality and the Muslim women were wearing clothes that were different from the Croat womens' clothes so they would be recognised, so they would not let them board buses, and I was recognised because I was well-known. So, they would not stop for me. There was an HVO soldier even, he was -- he showed up once when one of the 13 times when I was threatened and once he threatened and he said: "If you do not leave, you will be killed", and I went to report that. And often times when I was going to work, he would pass by in a car and he would show like this with a finger, as if I was a child, threatening me and I went to the Battalion Officer and made a report and then Mila Militic from Presevic came to me and said to me: "You must not write any more reports". When I showed up, he showed me a report written in English. This soldier who showed me this was Mato Tomic called Hercegovac showed me a copy of this, so that I did not feel safe, even walking on foot, so I always walked on the edge of the road because I thought that I would be -- I may be ran over by an oncoming vehicle, or I could jump into a ditch, so I -- I always feared that they would take everything away from us, that they would leave us with nothing. They simply took everything away from us, all our belongings and I apologise for what I am going to say; I do not know if you civilised people can understand it. I was in a situation in this Croat house, I had to wear underwear, women's underwear that I found in the house, it was somebody else's underwear, we were like beggars, we had nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did all Muslims had to leave Gromiljak, most of them left or some stayed and some left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some managed to escape. The majority ended up in camps and I was fortunate enough that I was not detained in a camp, even though I had heard that there were plans for me to be taken to the Rotilj camp, but, as I said previously, I was eventually exchanged in a small exchange, so I was not in the camp myself, but those who were in the camp tell horrifying stories about what happened to them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Witness LL, you said that Chief of the HVO Police offered you his house. To your knowledge, did other Croats offer any houses or any other form of assistance to other Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The Chief of Police offered me his house in order to cover up what was happening in front of Colonel Craig Carrington, because my impression was, every time when I went to UNPROFOR to report on what happened, my impression was they did not know what was happening, because all UNPROFOR interpreters were Croats so most probably they did not translate what was necessary, what had to be translated, but what was to their advantage. But, because I could manage, I spoke some English, I managed to talk to them. Velimir Milicevic tried to hide what was happening, he then after -- I spoke directly to Mr. Carrington, he offered me his house, but I did not want to go to his house, his family was away in Split because his house was just across the building where the people who beat me were staying, so it was pointless for me to go to his house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So, you are not disposed to credit him with acting out of kindness to you in offering you his house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think he was not honest. He simply wanted to put me away. He wanted to finish with this UN official as soon as possible. He would have probably evicted me on the same afternoon or would have sent someone to throw me out of his house because he was in the position of authority to other policemen, he was their chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me turn to your reference to the Washington Agreement of February 1954 (sic), you said that it was followed by the destruction of a number of mosques. In your mind, did you then see a relationship between the Washington Agreement and the destruction of the mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did see a relationship, because someone was supposed to take care of the implementation of the Washington Agreement and they knew that later on they would not have the opportunity to destroy property, so they did at the very beginning, immediately after the signing of the Agreement, they wanted to do it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Now, you also said that I think you saw a number of houses on fire. Were they Muslim houses or Croat houses or partly one and partly the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only Muslim houses. Exclusively Muslim houses, not a single Croat house was ever on fire. In the village of Gomjanica, which was a Muslim village, there were several Croat houses, maybe two or three and they remained standing, not a single bullet was shot at them. The targets were only Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Last question: you said that lots of people were killed. These people who were killed, were they Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Muslim civilians, all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, we have reached the end, Witness LL. You have responded to all of the questions put to you, and the Tribunal thanks you. We hope for you that you will be able, in the weeks and the months to come, be able to find the serenity that you deserve. Please do not move for the time being, because you are a protected witness. It will be the Registry which will tell you when you should move and how you should proceed. As far as the time is concerned, the judges are going to take a 20-minute recess, approximately 20 minutes. So the Chamber now stands adjourned. (4.20 pm) (A short break) (4.48 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are now resuming. Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harman, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. The next witness is a protected witness and we are going to be requesting that we proceed with a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No observations from the Defence? Okay, how are we going to call this witness; Witness MM, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Tuesday, 5th May 1998)
